latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Activation of drug- or drug-metabolite-specific CD8+ (and to lesser extent CD4+) T cells presenting via specific HLA alleles (e.g., HLA-B*5801/allopurinol, HLA-B*1502/carbamazepine, HLA-A*3101/carbamazepine, HLA-B*5701/abacavir). Core upstream driver of DRESS that initiates systemic inflammation, eosinophil expansion, and organ infiltration.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Reactive drug metabolite accumulation due to detoxification defect
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Slow acetylator phenotype, epoxide hydrolase or glutathione S-transferase deficiency leads to accumulation of reactive arene-oxide / nitroso metabolites (especially aromatic anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, dapsone). These haptenate self-proteins and prime drug-specific T-cell responses; explains delayed 2–8 week latency.

Sequential herpesvirus reactivation, classically HHV-6 around days 14–28, then HHV-7/EBV/CMV. Considered both a diagnostic hallmark and a driver of disease perpetuation, prolonged course, flares after drug withdrawal, and late autoimmune sequelae.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Th2-skewed cytokine response with IL-5–driven eosinophilia
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: T-cell activation in DRESS is skewed toward Th2 with IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, and TARC/CCL17 elevation. IL-5 drives bone-marrow eosinophil release and tissue eosinophil infiltration, accounting for the diagnostic eosinophilia and tissue eosinophil-rich infiltrates.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Systemic T-cell and eosinophil infiltration of visceral organs
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Drug-specific cytotoxic T cells and eosinophils infiltrate liver (hepatitis, most common visceral involvement), kidney (acute tubulointerstitial nephritis), lung (interstitial pneumonitis), heart (eosinophilic myocarditis, often delayed and a major cause of mortality), and brain. Drives organ-specific axes (ALT/AST, creatinine, troponin, oxygen saturation).

Months to years after acute DRESS, surviving patients are at risk for autoimmune thyroiditis (Graves/Hashimoto), fulminant type 1 diabetes, autoimmune hepatitis, SLE-like disease, and alopecia areata. Mechanism involves persistent dysregulated T-cell repertoire and viral reactivation footprints.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Secondary HLH/MAS-like macrophage activation in severe DRESS
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: A subset of severe DRESS evolves toward a hemophagocytic-like syndrome with hyperferritinemia, hypertriglyceridemia, cytopenias, and hepatic dysfunction. Driven by sustained T-cell/IFN-γ signaling and viral reactivation; predicts higher mortality and overlaps with sHLH workup.
Type-1 cytokine arm running in parallel to Th2 in DRESS, contributes to macrophage activation, hepatocyte injury and (in severe cases) HLH-like physiology.
Sustained IL-6 elevation driving fever, CRP, ferritin, and acute-phase proteins. Accounts for fever-of-unknown-origin presentation that often triggers infection workup.

Latent factor capturing how strongly the clinical picture (fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, organ dysfunction, occasional procalcitonin elevation) mimics bacterial sepsis or acute viral infection, driving diagnostic delay and inappropriate antibiotic exposure.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Reactive metabolites haptenate host proteins and are presented by HLA to drug-specific T cells; delayed accumulation explains the characteristic 2–8 week latency.
Activated T cells in DRESS preferentially produce IL-5/IL-4/IL-13, driving bone-marrow eosinophilopoiesis and tissue eosinophilia.
CD8+ T cell expansion drives IFN-γ and CXCL9/10 secretion contributing to hepatocyte injury and macrophage activation.
T-cell turnover and immune dysregulation permit HHV-6 reactivation, classically detectable 2–4 weeks after onset.
Reactivated HHV-6 expands cross-reactive virus- and drug-specific T cells, perpetuating immune activation and causing relapses even after drug withdrawal.
Viral reactivation footprint and altered T-cell repertoire predispose to autoimmune thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes, and SLE-like syndromes months after the acute event.
Activated drug-specific T cells traffic to liver, kidney, lung, and heart, producing organ-specific injury patterns.
IL-5 drives eosinophilopoiesis; eosinophil count >0.7 or >1.5×10^9/L is part of RegiSCAR criteria.
Reactive lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes is a RegiSCAR criterion alternative to eosinophilia.
Drug-specific T cells infiltrate dermis producing extensive morbilliform/maculopapular eruption typically covering >50% BSA, often progressing to erythroderma or exfoliation.
Periorbital and facial edema is a relatively specific clinical clue distinguishing DRESS from simple maculopapular drug eruptions.
Reactive T-cell expansion drives generalized lymphadenopathy at ≥2 sites (RegiSCAR criterion).
IL-6/IL-1 drive fever ≥38.5°C, often the first or earliest sign and a RegiSCAR criterion.
Acute-phase response elevates CRP, often raising suspicion for bacterial infection.
Hepatic involvement is the most common visceral manifestation (~75–95%) with hepatocellular or mixed pattern; ALT >2×ULN is part of RegiSCAR organ involvement.
Same hepatic infiltration pattern produces concurrent AST elevation; severe rises >10×ULN predict fulminant hepatitis and mortality.
Cholestatic or mixed hepatic injury patterns are common, especially with carbamazepine, minocycline, and dapsone-induced DRESS.
Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia accompanies severe DRESS hepatitis and predicts progression to acute liver failure.
Acute interstitial nephritis (especially with allopurinol- and vancomycin-induced DRESS) raises creatinine; urinary eosinophils may be present.

Eosinophilic and hypersensitivity myocarditis can occur weeks to months into the course (often after apparent improvement) and is a leading cause of late mortality. Troponin should be checked even when patients seem to be recovering.
Eosinophilic interstitial pneumonitis or ARDS may complicate severe DRESS, particularly with minocycline.
Eosinophilic/hypersensitivity myocarditis is a major late and often fatal complication, sometimes presenting weeks after rash and fever resolve.
Severe hepatic involvement is the leading cause of acute mortality in DRESS; coagulopathy and encephalopathy mark fulminant course.
Acute interstitial nephritis can progress to clinically significant AKI requiring dose adjustment and occasional renal replacement therapy.
Severe DRESS with HLH overlap shows ferritin often >2,000–10,000 ng/mL; useful prognostic marker.
Hypertriglyceridemia is one of the HLH-2004 criteria potentially fulfilled by severe DRESS evolving to MAS/HLH.
Macrophage activation and bone-marrow suppression cause thrombocytopenia in severe DRESS.
Severe DRESS can fulfill HLH-2004 criteria; mortality is markedly higher when this overlap occurs.
Autoimmune thyroiditis (silent, Graves, or Hashimoto) develops in ~5–10% of DRESS survivors; long-term thyroid surveillance is recommended.
Fulminant autoimmune T1DM presenting weeks-to-months after DRESS resolution is a recognized late complication.
Fever, rash, leukocytosis, and elevated CRP frequently trigger empiric antibiotics, which can themselves cross-react and worsen DRESS (e.g., adding β-lactams or sulfonamides).
Overall DRESS mortality is ~5–10%, mainly from hepatic failure, fulminant myocarditis, and HLH overlap.
Acute liver failure is the leading cause of acute DRESS mortality.
Eosinophilic myocarditis often presents late and can progress rapidly to cardiogenic shock; major contributor to mortality even after apparent clinical recovery.
Secondary HLH overlap markedly increases case-fatality rate in severe DRESS.

axes.shape_free_text: Baseline ~0.05–0.4 ×10^9/L; rises 2–6 weeks after drug initiation, often to 1.5–10 ×10^9/L; peaks around clinical onset; declines slowly over weeks to months. Eosinophil count >0.7 (mild) or >1.5 ×10^9/L (marked) is RegiSCAR criterion.
Reactive atypical lymphocytes appear during acute phase, often 5–20% of WBC differential; alternative RegiSCAR criterion to eosinophilia.
Often elevated (12–30 ×10^9/L) due to eosinophilia and lymphocytosis; less commonly leukopenic (especially with HLH overlap or marrow suppression).
Variable; usually preserved or mildly elevated. Severe forms or HLH overlap may cause neutropenia.
Usually normal in mild DRESS; thrombocytopenia indicates severe disease, HLH overlap, or DIC.
Mild normocytic anemia common (anemia of inflammation, marrow suppression).
High fever 38.5–40°C, often the earliest manifestation, persists for days–weeks even after drug withdrawal; may relapse with viral reactivation.
axes.second_peak: Possible relapsing fever during steroid taper or HHV-6/CMV reactivation

axes.shape_free_text: Sinus tachycardia from fever; persistent tachycardia or new arrhythmia raises concern for myocarditis.
Diffuse maculopapular/morbilliform eruption typically covering >50% BSA, may evolve to erythroderma, exfoliation, purpura, or pustules; commonly persists 2–6 weeks and may relapse during taper.
Periorbital and facial swelling is a relatively specific clue; occurs in ~50% of DRESS cases.
Often intense; persists for weeks.
Mild mucositis (cheilitis, conjunctivitis, mild oral ulcers) may occur in DRESS but is generally less severe than in SJS/TEN; prominent mucosal involvement should prompt overlap consideration.
Generalized non-tender or mildly tender lymphadenopathy at ≥2 sites (cervical, axillary, inguinal); part of RegiSCAR criteria.
Hepatomegaly with tenderness in patients with significant DRESS hepatitis; often subclinical.
Mild splenomegaly may be present, especially with HLH overlap.
Elevated in 75–95% of cases; commonly 2–10×ULN, may exceed 20×ULN in severe forms; hepatitis often peaks 2–6 weeks after drug start and can persist or relapse for months.
Tracks ALT; mixed hepatocellular pattern most common.
Cholestatic or mixed pattern especially with carbamazepine, minocycline, dapsone.
Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia in severe disease; >5 mg/dL with coagulopathy suggests acute liver failure.
Elevation indicates synthetic dysfunction; INR >1.5 with hepatitis defines severe hepatic involvement and predicts mortality.
Acute interstitial nephritis (allopurinol, vancomycin most common) can elevate creatinine; usually mild–moderate but occasionally requires renal replacement.
Should be checked in any patient with chest pain, dyspnea, hemodynamic instability, or persistent tachycardia; eosinophilic myocarditis can present 3 weeks to several months after onset.
Usually preserved; falls when eosinophilic pneumonitis or ARDS develops.
Often moderately to markedly elevated, mimicking infection; not a reliable discriminator from sepsis.
Usually normal or only mildly elevated in DRESS — a useful (though imperfect) discriminator from bacterial sepsis when CRP is high.
Often elevated; markedly elevated values (>2,000 ng/mL or in particular >10,000 ng/mL) suggest HLH overlap and worse prognosis.
Hypertriglyceridemia accompanies HLH-like overlap.
May fall in HLH overlap or DIC.
Elevated reflecting tissue inflammation/hemolysis or HLH overlap.
Substantially elevated, paralleling fever and CRP.
Marked T-cell activation marker; useful when HLH overlap suspected.

HHV-6 (and HHV-7/EBV/CMV) reactivation in plasma/whole blood typically detectable 2–4 weeks after symptom onset; supports diagnosis and predicts severe/relapsing course; chromosomal integrated HHV-6 must be distinguished.
EBV reactivation often follows HHV-6, in second to third month.
CMV reactivation can occur, especially in steroid-treated severe DRESS, predicting more complications.
Late-onset thyroid dysfunction (silent thyroiditis, Hashimoto, Graves) develops weeks to months after acute illness; thyroid surveillance for ≥6–12 months is recommended.

RegiSCAR score: ≥6 definite, 4–5 probable, 2–3 possible. Composite of fever, lymphadenopathy ≥2 sites, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes, skin involvement (extent, morphology, biopsy), organ involvement, resolution >15 days, exclusion of alternatives.
Hazard of fulminant autoimmune type 1 diabetes onset, sometimes presenting in DKA weeks to months after DRESS.
Hazard of evolution to acute liver failure, peaking when ALT/AST and bilirubin rise sharply with INR >1.5.
Eosinophilic/hypersensitivity myocarditis, often delayed; may present after fever and rash improve.
Hazard of clinically significant AKI from interstitial nephritis.
Hazard of fulfilling HLH-2004 criteria in severe DRESS.
Increased on prolonged corticosteroid/immunosuppressive therapy; opportunistic infections (CMV colitis, PJP, HSV) reported.

Overall case fatality ~5–10%; concentrated in severe hepatitis, fulminant myocarditis, and HLH-overlap cases. Hazard rises with severity scores, ALT >10×ULN, INR >1.5, bilirubin >5 mg/dL, hyperferritinemia, troponin elevation, and elderly host.
Probability that the febrile syndrome is bacterial sepsis rather than DRESS; usually low if delayed onset, characteristic rash, eosinophilia, normal procalcitonin, no clear focus.
Concurrent empiric β-lactam/sulfonamide/vancomycin given for presumed sepsis can perpetuate or worsen DRESS; high values worsen course.
Steroid-induced hyperglycemia, psychosis, hypertension, and infection risk during prolonged corticosteroid therapy required by severe DRESS.
Risk of HBV reactivation under prolonged corticosteroids; antiviral prophylaxis indicated in HBsAg+ or core+ patients.
Severe hepatic injury limits use of further hepatotoxic drugs and may favor non-hepatic-cleared adjuncts.
Severe AKI requires dose adjustment and avoidance of nephrotoxins.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Tissue eosinophil infiltration parallels hepatic injury; rising eosinophils often precede ALT elevation by days.
HHV-6 reactivation often coincides with relapsing fever and worsening rash, especially during steroid taper.
Viral reactivation aggravates hepatitis and predicts protracted disease.
Severe hepatocellular injury precedes synthetic dysfunction (rising INR), defining acute liver failure.
ALT/AST >10×ULN with rising bilirubin and INR signals impending acute liver failure.
Even modest troponin elevation in DRESS warrants urgent cardiac MRI/biopsy as eosinophilic myocarditis can progress rapidly.
Hyperferritinemia (>2,000–10,000 ng/mL) with cytopenias and hypertriglyceridemia signals HLH overlap.
Higher RegiSCAR scores and number/severity of organ involvements correlate with mortality.
PCT typically remains low in DRESS; markedly elevated values shift posterior toward bacterial sepsis or superinfection.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: All structurally related drugs (e.g., aromatic anticonvulsants cross-react: phenytoin/carbamazepine/phenobarbital/oxcarbazepine; aromatic amines: sulfonamides) must be stopped to halt antigenic drive.

failure_modes: continued exposure to cross-reactive agents (e.g., carbamazepine after phenytoin)
course continues for weeks despite withdrawal due to HHV-6 reactivation
treatments.context_specific_role: Mandatory in every DRESS case; alone insufficient when severe organ involvement exists.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe hepatitis (>5×ULN) is a clear indication for systemic corticosteroids 0.5–1 mg/kg/day.
Suspected eosinophilic myocarditis often warrants pulse methylprednisolone 0.5–1 g/day for 3 days.
Long-course steroids in HBV-positive patients require antiviral prophylaxis.
If sepsis is still possible, prefer empiric antimicrobials and rapid de-escalation rather than upfront high-dose steroids.

failure_modes: premature taper triggering relapse (very common; tapers should run 3–6+ months)
viral reactivation flares during taper (HHV-6, CMV)
opportunistic infection on prolonged immunosuppression (PJP, CMV)

side_effects.interpretation: Steroid-induced hyperglycemia, occasionally precipitating new diabetes
Increased opportunistic infection risk on prolonged therapy

treatments.context_specific_role: Standard for moderate–severe DRESS (significant hepatitis, nephritis, pneumonitis, myocarditis, RegiSCAR-defined severe disease). Slow taper over 3–6 months recommended to prevent relapse.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Mild DRESS without significant organ involvement may be managed with topical steroids plus supportive care alone, avoiding systemic immunosuppression.

treatments.context_specific_role: First-line skin-directed therapy in mild DRESS without RegiSCAR-defined severe organ involvement.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Nephrotoxicity makes cyclosporine challenging in patients with significant DRESS-related AKI.

treatments.context_specific_role: Steroid-sparing or steroid-resistant cases; some emerging evidence for short courses (3–5 mg/kg/day for 1 week) in moderate DRESS.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe steroid-resistant DRESS or HLH overlap may benefit from IVIG in combination with steroids.

failure_modes: monotherapy in severe DRESS may be inferior to steroids
thromboembolism, aseptic meningitis, AKI in high-dose use
treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunct to corticosteroids in severe/refractory DRESS, especially with HLH overlap; not recommended as monotherapy.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: High HHV-6 viremia with ongoing organ involvement may justify antiviral therapy, though evidence is limited.
Established CMV reactivation with end-organ disease (colitis, pneumonitis) warrants ganciclovir.
Ganciclovir myelotoxicity can worsen pre-existing neutropenia.

failure_modes: limited evidence base for HHV-6 in DRESS
treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunctive therapy for severe DRESS with documented HHV-6/CMV/EBV reactivation and end-organ disease.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Standard adjunct in non-acetaminophen acute liver failure; modestly improves transplant-free survival.

failure_modes: does not replace transplant evaluation in fulminant cases
treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunct in DRESS with severe hepatitis or developing acute liver failure.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: INR >1.5 with encephalopathy meets King's College criteria threshold for transplant evaluation.

treatments.context_specific_role: Reserved for fulminant DRESS hepatitis meeting transplant criteria.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: When sepsis cannot be excluded (e.g., neutropenia, hypotension, focal source) empiric coverage is justified pending workup.
In classic DRESS without sepsis features, empiric antibiotics may worsen the eruption and complicate culprit identification; avoid β-lactams/sulfonamides whenever possible.

side_effects.interpretation: Adding cross-reactive antibiotics can perpetuate rash and organ injury

treatments.context_specific_role: Used when sepsis genuinely cannot be excluded; otherwise minimized and chosen from non-cross-reactive classes.
Maintain perfusion and renal flow; cautious in suspected myocarditis.

positive.trajectory_modulation: Strongly increases risk of allopurinol-induced DRESS/SJS/TEN, especially in Han Chinese, Korean, and Thai populations; pre-treatment screening recommended in these groups.
Risk for carbamazepine-induced severe cutaneous adverse reactions including DRESS in Han Chinese, Thai, Malaysian, Indian populations; pre-treatment screening mandated in many countries.
Carbamazepine-induced DRESS especially in Europeans and Japanese; also associated with phenytoin DRESS.
Abacavir hypersensitivity / DRESS-like reaction; pre-treatment screening required.

slow.trajectory_modulation: Reduced metabolism of sulfonamides, dapsone, isoniazid increases reactive metabolite exposure.

yes.trajectory_modulation: Especially with renal dysfunction or HLA-B*5801; doses >300 mg/day amplify risk.
Increasingly recognized DRESS culprit, especially with prolonged courses ≥2 weeks.
Often associated with prolonged eosinophilic pneumonitis and autoimmune sequelae.
Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome essentially overlaps DRESS, characteristic methemoglobinemia and hemolysis.
Isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide can each precipitate DRESS, often with overlapping hepatotoxicity.

egfr_below_60.trajectory_modulation: Particularly amplifies allopurinol DRESS risk via metabolite accumulation.

yes.trajectory_modulation: Greatly increased risk with sulfonamides, nevirapine, abacavir; immune dysregulation predisposes.

elderly.trajectory_modulation: Older age associated with higher mortality, more severe hepatic/cardiac involvement.

yes.trajectory_modulation: Higher carrier frequency of HLA-B*1502, HLA-B*5801 increases population risk for carbamazepine and allopurinol DRESS/SCAR.

supportive_care: Identify and immediately stop the offending drug and all structurally related cross-reactive drugs; document on the patient's allergy list and educate the patient and family
Admit patients with severe DRESS (significant hepatitis, AKI, pneumonitis, myocarditis, hemodynamic instability, or HLH overlap) to a unit capable of organ support
Use the RegiSCAR scoring system to stratify probable/definite DRESS and guide treatment intensity

Daily monitoring during the acute phase: temperature, vital signs, body surface area of rash, organ exam (liver, lymph nodes), full blood count with differential (eosinophils, atypical lymphocytes), liver enzymes (ALT, AST, ALP, bilirubin), creatinine, urinalysis, CRP, ferritin, troponin if any cardiac symptoms or persistent tachycardia
Baseline and serial HHV-6 PCR (and HHV-7, EBV, CMV when severe or relapsing) to support diagnosis and identify viral reactivation contributing to relapses
Baseline and follow-up thyroid function (TSH, free T4) and fasting glucose for at least 6–12 months to detect autoimmune thyroiditis and fulminant type 1 diabetes
ECG and echocardiogram (with cardiac MRI if clinically suspicious) to screen for eosinophilic myocarditis, especially with troponin elevation, dyspnea, chest pain, or persistent tachycardia
Baseline HBV serology (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs); start antiviral prophylaxis (e.g., entecavir/tenofovir) before prolonged corticosteroid therapy in HBV-positive patients
Skin care: bland emollients, high-potency topical steroids, careful temperature regulation, avoidance of secondary infection of skin breakdown
Avoid empiric β-lactams, sulfonamides, vancomycin, and minocycline unless absolutely required; use non-cross-reactive antimicrobials guided by cultures when infection is genuinely suspected
Pain control with non-NSAID, non-cross-reactive analgesics; avoid NSAIDs in patients with AKI

When systemic corticosteroids are used: taper slowly over 3–6+ months; provide PJP prophylaxis (e.g., atovaquone if sulfonamides contraindicated), bone protection, glycemic monitoring, blood pressure monitoring, ophthalmologic surveillance for prolonged courses
Watch for and counsel patients about relapse during taper (re-emergence of fever, rash, eosinophilia, or transaminitis often correlating with viral reactivation)

Refer to dermatology and clinical immunology/allergy for confirmation and long-term cross-reactivity advice; patch testing and lymphocyte transformation testing may help identify the culprit when the offender is uncertain

Genetic screening (HLA-B*5801 before allopurinol in high-risk populations; HLA-B*1502 before carbamazepine in Han Chinese and related populations; HLA-B*5701 before abacavir) is the primary primary-prevention strategy
Provide written documentation listing the culprit drug and all cross-reactive agents; advise medical alert bracelet and inform pharmacy/electronic medical record
Long-term follow-up at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months for autoimmune sequelae (thyroid, diabetes, lupus-like, autoimmune hepatitis, alopecia areata, vitiligo)
Psychosocial support: prolonged hospitalization, body image impact of erythroderma and post-inflammatory pigmentation, fear of future drug reactions
